issues.item: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: 'Talks or photos about snakes' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another unless the accident specifically involved a snake, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items point to generic post-traumatic cueing, but this item implies a highly specific trauma cue that lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another and is not supported by the other nodes. The profile otherwise centers on guilt, danger scanning, intrusive recollection, and distrust of self/body; betrayal by another person introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme without corroboration.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Avoiding emotional closeness/intimacy is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The dominant threat and memory items concern danger, hypervigilance, intrusive imagery, numbness, and grief after an accidental injury event. Intimacy avoidance could occur, but here it appears to address an interpersonal/betrayal theme that is not otherwise coherently represented, especially given the unsupported betrayal appraisal.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by generalized interpersonal/environmental danger monitoring (avoiding unfamiliar places, scanning exits in any room), which fits assault or deliberate threat contexts better than accidentally causing serious injury to another in an accident. For this trauma type, threat is more plausibly focused on accidents, loss of control, or harm recurrence rather than pervasive escape-oriented vigilance across all settings.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I can't rely on other people' is weakly grounded in the rest of the profile. The other nodes center on accident-related triggers, guilt, bodily unreliability, and generalized hypervigilance, but there is no corresponding interpersonal betrayal, abandonment, or dependence theme to support this item. It stands out as clinically disconnected from the trauma narrative and the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Mai was nineteen and working as a hairdresser at a salon in a strip mall when the accident happened. She had been driving home after a long shift, her mind still half on the client who had wanted a complicated balayage, when she saw the boy-maybe seven years old-break away from his mother on the sidewalk and sprint straight into the crosswalk without looking. Mai slammed the brakes, but the car hit him. The sound of the impact was a dull, heavy thud that seemed to come from inside her own chest, and then the screaming started-the mother's scream, the boy's thin wail, the screech of the tires on the asphalt still ringing in her ears. She got out of the car and saw him lying on the ground, his leg bent at an angle that made her stomach turn. She dialed 911 with shaking hands, and while she waited, she kept saying "I'm sorry" over and over, but the words felt useless. The boy survived, but the doctors said he would need multiple surgeries and might never walk normally again. Mai was never charged-the family's lawyer made it clear the boy had run out without warning-but that did not matter to her.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of the accident came back to her not as a story she could tell but as a series of pictures that appeared without warning: the boy's startled face just before impact, the unnatural angle of his leg, the mother's hands flying up to her mouth. Loud noises of any kind could set it off-a car horn in traffic, a door slamming in the salon-and she would feel her heart race, her palms go slick with sweat, and for a moment she would be right back on that street corner. Sometimes, when the images came, she would feel nothing at all. She would recall the whole scene with a strange, hollow numbness, as if it had happened to someone else, as if she were watching a movie. And then, just as suddenly, the grief would hit her-a raw, wordless sorrow that made her want to curl up on the floor and cry for that boy and his mother and for herself, for the person she used to be before she had done this. When the first anniversary of the accident approached, Mai found herself shrinking from the date itself. She took it off work by telling her manager she had a family obligation, then spent the whole day alone in her apartment with the blinds closed, refusing to step outside because the calendar felt like an accusation-a yearly marker of the moment she had ruined a child's life. She did not tell her boyfriend why she had made herself unavailable; she was certain he would try to offer comfort she did not deserve, and she could not bear the thought of that. The following year, she scheduled a double shift at the salon for that exact date, forcing herself to stay busy, but the dread still coiled in her stomach for weeks beforehand.

Mai stopped driving completely. She also stopped being a passenger. When her boyfriend offered to drive her to work, she said no, each time feeling a tight knot of fear in her chest at the thought of sitting in a car with someone else at the wheel-she was certain that any driver could make a mistake, that a momentary lapse in attention could cause another accident, and she would be helpless, unable to do anything but watch. She began walking to the salon instead, even though it took over an hour each way, her legs aching by the time she arrived. She stopped taking the bus altogether, which meant her world shrank to the few places she could reach on foot: work, the small corner store two blocks from her apartment, her building's laundry room. She stopped seeing friends who lived farther away, stopped going to the grocery store unless her boyfriend offered to buy things for her, and even then she would feel a wave of guilt and anxiety, certain she was becoming a burden. She refused to let him drive her anywhere, not even to a nearby restaurant, because being a passenger had come to feel as dangerous as driving-she could not trust anyone else to keep them safe. Her boyfriend grew confused and frustrated, asking why she would rather walk miles in the cold than accept a ride, and Mai could not explain that her body had become a liability, that she no longer trusted either herself or anyone else to be safe behind the wheel.

At the salon, Mai became excessively compliant. When a client complained about the cut, she apologized and offered a free redo even when the cut was fine. When her coworker asked her to stay late, she said yes even though she was exhausted. She had come to believe that she could not trust herself-if her own body could cause such harm without her intending it, then she had no right to assert herself, to say no. She had failed to protect that boy, so she would try to protect everyone else now by never causing any friction, never being a problem. This fawn response had started to drain her. She would go home and lie on the couch, unable to relax even in her own bedroom, because she was always scanning for threats. In the salon, she had memorized the location of every exit the first day she returned to work. In a restaurant with her boyfriend-on the rare occasions she agreed to go, and only if they walked there-she would sit facing the door, her eyes darting to the back hallway every few minutes. He had started to ask why she seemed so on edge, and she did not know how to explain that her body had become a liability, that she no longer trusted herself to be safe around others-and that even as she accepted his offers to buy groceries, she was bracing for the moment he would stop, because she was certain that no one could be counted on forever.

What finally brought Mai to seek help was a panic attack that hit her in the middle of a haircut. A client had brought her toddler, and the child slipped off the chair and let out a sharp cry. Mai heard it and froze, the sound dissolving into the memory of the boy's wail. She dropped her scissors and had to run to the back room, her hands shaking, her chest tight. The salon manager asked if she was okay, and Mai said yes, but she knew she was not. She made an appointment with a therapist that afternoon, though part of her was already skeptical that talking would help-why would a stranger be any different from everyone else who had told her it was not her fault but could not actually make her believe it? What she was most afraid of, she told herself, was that she would never feel normal again-that she would always be this version of herself, jumpy, compliant, grieving, unable to trust either herself or the people around her, trapped in a shrinking world she could only reach on foot, and that each coming anniversary would pull her back into the same numbness and dread. But what she hoped for, in a small and barely acknowledged corner of her mind, was that someone could help her understand why she could not let the accident go, even though everyone else had told her it was not her fault.

Mai was nineteen and working as a hairdresser at a salon in a strip mall when the accident happened. She had been driving home after a long shift, her mind still half on the client who had wanted a complicated balayage, when she saw the boy—maybe seven years old—break away from his mother on the sidewalk and sprint straight into the crosswalk without looking. Mai slammed the brakes, but the car hit him. The sound of the impact was a dull, heavy thud that seemed to come from inside her own chest, and then the screaming started—the mother's scream, the boy's thin wail, the screech of the tires on the asphalt still ringing in her ears. She got out of the car and saw him lying on the ground, his leg bent at an angle that made her stomach turn. She dialed 911 with shaking hands, and while she waited, she kept saying "I'm sorry" over and over, but the words felt useless. The boy survived, but the doctors said he would need multiple surgeries and might never walk normally again. Mai was never charged—the family's lawyer made it clear the boy had run out without warning—but that did not matter to her.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of the accident came back to her not as a story she could tell but as a series of pictures that appeared without warning: the boy's startled face just before impact, the unnatural angle of his leg, the mother's hands flying up to her mouth. Loud noises of any kind could set it off—a car horn in traffic, a door slamming in the salon—and she would feel her heart race, her palms go slick with sweat, and for a moment she would be right back on that street corner. Sometimes, when the images came, she would feel nothing at all. She would recall the whole scene with a strange, hollow numbness, as if it had happened to someone else, as if she were watching a movie. And then, just as suddenly, the grief would hit her—a raw, wordless sorrow that made her want to curl up on the floor and cry for that boy and his mother and for herself, for the person she used to be before she had done this. When the first anniversary of the accident approached, Mai found herself shrinking from the date itself. She took it off work by telling her manager she had a family obligation, then spent the whole day alone in her apartment with the blinds closed, refusing to step outside because the calendar felt like an accusation—a yearly marker of the moment she had ruined a child's life. She did not tell her boyfriend why she had made herself unavailable; she was certain he would try to offer comfort she did not deserve, and she could not bear the thought of that. The following year, she scheduled a double shift at the salon for that exact date, forcing herself to stay busy, but the dread still coiled in her stomach for weeks beforehand.

Mai stopped driving completely. She also stopped being a passenger. When her boyfriend offered to drive her to work, she said no, each time feeling a tight knot of fear in her chest at the thought of sitting in a car with someone else at the wheel—she was certain that any driver could make a mistake, that a momentary lapse in attention could cause another accident, and she would be helpless, unable to do anything but watch. She began walking to the salon instead, even though it took over an hour each way, her legs aching by the time she arrived. She stopped taking the bus altogether, which meant her world shrank to the few places she could reach on foot: work, the small corner store two blocks from her apartment, her building's laundry room. She stopped seeing friends who lived farther away, stopped going to the grocery store unless her boyfriend offered to buy things for her, and even then she would feel a wave of guilt and anxiety, certain she was becoming a burden. She refused to let him drive her anywhere, not even to a nearby restaurant, because being a passenger had come to feel as dangerous as driving—she could not trust anyone else to keep them safe. Her boyfriend grew confused and frustrated, asking why she would rather walk miles in the cold than accept a ride, and Mai could not explain that her body had become a liability, that she no longer trusted either herself or anyone else to be safe behind the wheel.

At the salon, Mai became excessively compliant. When a client complained about the cut, she apologized and offered a free redo even when the cut was fine. When her coworker asked her to stay late, she said yes even though she was exhausted. She had come to believe that she could not trust herself—if her own body could cause such harm without her intending it, then she had no right to assert herself, to say no. She had failed to protect that boy, so she would try to protect everyone else now by never causing any friction, never being a problem. This fawn response had started to drain her. She would go home and lie on the couch, unable to relax even in her own bedroom, because she was always scanning for threats. In the salon, she had memorized the location of every exit the first day she returned to work. In a restaurant with her boyfriend—on the rare occasions she agreed to go, and only if they walked there—she would sit facing the door, her eyes darting to the back hallway every few minutes. He had started to ask why she seemed so on edge, and she did not know how to explain that her body had become a liability, that she no longer trusted herself to be safe around others—and that even as she accepted his offers to buy groceries, she was bracing for the moment he would stop, because she was certain that no one could be counted on forever.

What finally brought Mai to seek help was a panic attack that hit her in the middle of a haircut. A client had brought her toddler, and the child slipped off the chair and let out a sharp cry. Mai heard it and froze, the sound dissolving into the memory of the boy's wail. She dropped her scissors and had to run to the back room, her hands shaking, her chest tight. The salon manager asked if she was okay, and Mai said yes, but she knew she was not. She made an appointment with a therapist that afternoon, though part of her was already skeptical that talking would help—why would a stranger be any different from everyone else who had told her it was not her fault but could not actually make her believe it? What she was most afraid of, she told herself, was that she would never feel normal again—that she would always be this version of herself, jumpy, compliant, grieving, unable to trust either herself or the people around her, trapped in a shrinking world she could only reach on foot, and that each coming anniversary would pull her back into the same numbness and dread. But what she hoped for, in a small and barely acknowledged corner of her mind, was that someone could help her understand why she could not let the accident go, even though everyone else had told her it was not her fault.
